chunks: What is pick-and-place. The question: What is pick-and-place?
Pick-and-place is the machine that puts surface-mount parts (parts that sit flat on the board) onto a board.

It picks each part from a feeder with a small suction nozzle, checks the part with a camera, and sets it down at the right spot and angle on the wet solder paste, a sticky mix of solder powder printed on the board.
It does this for every part on the board, very quickly.
Think of a claw machine at an arcade, but one that is fast and precise, and always grabs the right prize.
A suction tip lifts a part off a reel of parts, a camera glances at how it is sitting on the tip, and the arm corrects before setting it down.
The sticky paste holds each part in place until the oven melts it. Unlike a claw machine, it never presses hard, because pushing too hard would squeeze the paste out.
The program supplies target X, Y, rotation; the part camera measures the actual pose on the nozzle; the head corrects before it places on the board whose position was found from fiducials.
Feeder: a holder that presents one part at a time, usually from a tape reel. Nozzle: the suction tip that picks up and releases a part.
Centroid file: a list from the design software giving each part's X and Y position, angle and board side. Fiducials: alignment dots the camera uses to find the board.
CPH: components per hour, the machine's speed rating.
Say a machine is rated at 20,000 parts per hour. One part then takes 3600 / 20,000 = 0. 18 seconds on average. A board with 400 parts needs 400 x 0. 18 = 72 seconds of placement.
A faster machine at 80,000 parts per hour would need only 18 seconds. Real speeds are lower than the rating, because of reel changes and awkward parts. That is the whole idea.
"Pick-and-place is the machine that puts surface-mount components on a board.

A vacuum nozzle picks a part from a feeder, usually a tape reel, a camera checks its position, and the head places it on the paste-printed pads at the programmed X, Y and rotation, using fiducials to align to the board.
A centroid file from CAD tells it where each part goes. Chip shooters place passives at tens of thousands per hour; flexible machines handle big or odd parts more slowly."
